§ 2Content

§ 3NATIONAL INCOME

  • National income is the total value of all goods and services produced by a country's residents in a given year. It is a "Macroeconomic" concept.
  • For the first time, the concept of National Income was given by Dadabhai Naoroji.
  • P.C. Mahalanobis headed the National Income Committee (1949).

Circular Flow of Income

  • The Circular Flow of Income is a model/concept often used to describe the continuous movement of goods, services, resources, and money in an economy.
  • Households own land, labor, and capital. They provide these to firms in return for income (wages, rent, profits).
  • Firms use these resources to produce goods and services and sell them to households.
  • Households spend money to buy goods and services from firms (expenditure).
  • Firms pay money to households for the resources they use (income).
  • This cycle keeps the economy moving by maintaining a continuous flow.

Flow Chart 1: Circular flow of income (Product method, Goods and services, Expenditure method, Consumer expenditure, Income method, Factors for production, Households, Firms)

Injection (Money Entering the Economy)

  • Injections are additional funds that enter the economy, increasing the total spending and income. They help expand economic activity.

Types

  • Investment: When businesses spend money on capital goods like machinery or buildings to expand production.
  • Government Spending: Public sector expenditure on goods and services like infrastructure, education, or defense.
  • Exports: Sales of domestic goods and services to foreign buyers, bringing money into the domestic economy.

More injections → Economic growth increases

Leakage (Money Leaving the Economy)

  • Leakages are funds that exit the circular flow, reducing total spending and slowing economic growth.

Types

  • Savings: When households save instead of spending their income.
  • Taxes: When people pay taxes to the government.
  • Imports: When people spend money on foreign-produced goods and services.

More leakages → Slower economic growth

In two sector economy, there is no leakage and no injection.

Three Methods to Calculate National Income

1. Value Added Method/Production Method/Output Method

  • It is a way to calculate the value of a product or service at each stage of production. It is also known as production method.

Value added method = Output - Input

Example:

CottonYarnClothShirt
Rs 100Rs 200Rs 400Rs 800
Value added in every stageRs 100Rs 100Rs 200Rs 400
  • Gross Value Added (GVA): The value that producers add to goods and services they buy and sell.

GVA = GVA₁ + GVA₂ + GVA₃ + ......GVA₈ (8 sectors per NSO)

Central Statistics Office (CSO) adopted the GVA in 2015

2. Income Method

  • This method includes all the income generated by the factors of production which are inputs in the process of producing final goods or services, in the entire economy.

Components of Income Method

  1. 1. Compensation to Employees: It refers to the total wages or salaries paid to workers for their product services.
  2. 2. Operating Surplus: It refers to the profit earned by businesses (profit, rent and interest) after deducting employees compensation (wages).
  3. 3. Mixed Income: It is the income earned by self-employed individuals and unincorporated businesses. It arises when elements of factor income (labour and capital) cannot be distinctly separated. E.g. A doctor running their own clinic.

3. Expenditure Method

  • It is way to calculate a country's GDP by adding up all spending on goods and services in the economy. It's the most common method for calculating GDP.

Expenditure Method = C + G + I + (X-M)

  • C = Consumption
  • G = Government Expenditure
  • I = Investment
  • X = Export
  • M = Import

Final Goods vs Intermediate Goods

Final GoodsIntermediate Goods
These goods will now not undergo any economic processThese are semi-finished products that will undergo various economic process and transformation to be converted to final products
Goods used by the consumer for personal consumption or investmentGoods used as inputs for producing other goods and services and will get customised in the process
Direct consumption or capital investmentFurther processing or resale
E.g. When you buy tea from a shop for personal consumption, it is a final goodE.g. When a tea shop or hotel buys tea to prepare and sell tea to customers, it becomes an intermediate good

Types of Final Goods

  • Consumer goods: Finished products used by individuals for personal consumption rather than for producing other goods.
  • Capital goods: They are physical goods used by businesses to produce other goods and services, but they do not get consumed in the process. E.g. Machine to produce T-shirts.

Inventory

  • It refers to the items a business keeps in stock for sale or production purposes. It can include raw materials, work-in-progress items, and finished goods, depending on the type of business.
  • If the sale of goods increases the inventory decumulates and if the sale of goods decreases the inventory accumulates. It can be either planned or unplanned.

Stock vs Flow

StockFlow
It is a quantity measured at a point of timeIt is a quantity measured over a period of time
Ex: Wealth, loan, inventory, capital, Money SupplyEx: Income, expenditure, change in inventory, depreciation

§ 4AGGREGATES OF NATIONAL INCOME

Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

  • GDP measures total value of all final goods and services produced within the territory of a country within a financial year (Financial Year: 1st April-31 March).

In GDP second hand goods are never counted.

  • While calculating GDP, value of only final goods is considered and not intermediate goods to avoid Double Counting.

Gross National Product (GNP)

  • Total value of all final goods and services produced by the nationals of the country.

Work done by women at home is outside the purview of GDP.

Net Domestic Product (NDP)

  • It is the measure of a country's economic output after adjusting for the depreciation (or consumption) of fixed capital.

GDP = GDP - Factor Income to Abroad + FI from Abroad

OR

GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)

  • Monetary Value of an Asset decreases over time due to various factors and is called as Depreciation. It is seen in Capital Goods.

NDP = GDP - Depreciation

Net National Product (NNP)

  • It is the monetary value of finished goods and services produced by a country's citizens in a given period.

NNP = GNP - Depreciation

GDP was developed by Russian-American Economist "Simon Kuznets" in 1934.

Market Price vs Factor Cost

Market Price (MP)Factor Cost (FC)
The market price is the final value of the product being sold, which includes indirect taxesFactor cost is the cost of factors of production, or total value of inputs, where indirect tax is not included

FC = MP - Indirect tax + Subsidy

FC = MP - (Indirect tax - Subsidy)

FC = MP - Net Indirect Tax

Basic Price = FC + Net production tax

Net production tax = (Production tax - Subsidy)

To Summarise

  1. 1. Gross में Net में आना हो तो Depreciation subtract करदो।
  2. 2. Domestic में National में आना हो तो NFIA add करदो।
  3. 3. MP से FC में आना हो तो Net Indirect Tax को substract करदो।

Real GDP vs Nominal GDP

Real GDPNominal GDP
In this, a base year is taken as referenceIt is more than Real GDP due to inflation
It is calculated on constant pricesIt is calculated on current prices
It is inflation adjustedInflation is not adjusted here

GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100

Current Base Year is 2011-2012, but the govt. has setup a committee to revise the Base Year to 2022-2023.

  • GDP Deflator is also called as "Implicit Price Deflation" and "Price Index".
  • GDP of India is calculated by: Central Statistical Officer (CSO) under Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).
  • The Base Year is considered as: 2011-2012.

Per Capita Income

  • It is the average amount of money earned by each person in a specific area over a period of time.

Per Capita Income = National Income / Population

Purchasing Power Parity

  • Purchasing power is the amount of goods and services that can be bought with a specific amount of money. It can also be referred to as "a common basket of goods".
  • As of 2024, India's GDP ranked 5th in the world and India's economy ranks at 3rd position in the world in terms of Purchasing Power Parity after USA and China (their economy is inflated).

Personal Income

  • Total income of an individual earned from all the sources before taxes.

Ranking of GDP (around the world)

  1. 1. USA
  2. 2. China
  3. 3. Germany
  4. 4. Japan
  5. 5. India

PI = National Income (NI) + Income received but not earned - Income earned but not received

OR

PI = NI + Govt. transfers + Net interest paid by Govt. - Corporate tax - payment for social security

PI = NI + Transfer Payment - Undistributed corporate profit

Transfer payment example: Government subsidies/Scholarship/Pension

Personal Disposable Income

  • It is the amount of money a person has after paying taxes and other mandatory withholding.

Disposable Income = Personal Income - Tax

Green GDP = GDP - Environmental Damage

Potential GDP - Real GDP = Recessionary Gap

Potential GDP

  • It is the total output an economy would produce if its resources are fully utilised.

V.K.R.V. Rao used a scientific approach to calculate National Income. He also gave two-sector economy classification.
